questions.question: What three primitives does an MCP server expose?
questions.explanation: The lesson defines an MCP server as exposing exactly three primitives: tools (functions the model calls), resources (read-only content addressed by URI), and prompts (reusable templated prompts).

questions.question: What wire format does MCP use?
questions.explanation: The lesson states MCP messages are JSON-RPC 2.0 over stdio, WebSocket, or streamable HTTP, with the format `{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "method": "...", "params": {...}, "id": N}`.

questions.question: In MCP terminology, what is the relationship between host, client, and server?
options: The host is the LLM application; the client is a sub-component of the host that speaks to exactly one server; the server is your code exposing tools, resources, and prompts
The host and client are the same thing; the server is the LLM itself
The server is the LLM application; the host exposes tools to it
The client is the protocol version; host and server are interchangeable terms for the same process
questions.explanation: The lesson defines the host as the LLM application (e.g. Claude Desktop), the client as a sub-component of the host that speaks to exactly one server, and the server as the code exposing tools, resources, and prompts. One host can mount many servers, each through its own client.

questions.question: What is the 2025-06-18 transport that replaced the earlier SSE-only remote transport?
questions.explanation: The lesson's wire-format section lists streamable HTTP, alongside stdio and WebSocket, as a transport for MCP's JSON-RPC 2.0 messages; of the four options, it is the only one the lesson names.

questions.question: When should a tool be split into its own MCP server instead of staying inline?
options: When it is called fewer than 10 times per day
When it is called from two or more hosts and is read-only/cacheable
When it returns more than 1KB of data
Never; MCP is only for local dev
